title: Checkpoint 6 Science: The Test and How to Prepare
kicker: Cambridge Primary Checkpoint · Science 0097 · Start here
summary: Everything you need to know about the Cambridge Primary Checkpoint Science test — the two papers, the question styles, how the mark scheme works — and how to use this course to get ready.

blocks.title: In the curriculum
items: This course covers the whole Cambridge Primary Science Stage 6 curriculum (framework code 0097).
Biology: the heart and blood, the lungs, growing up, diseases and hygiene, food webs (6Bs, 6Bp, 6Be)
Chemistry: properties of substances, reversible changes, dissolving, boiling and evaporation, chemical reactions (6Cp, 6Cc)
Physics: mass and weight, forces, floating and sinking, light, electric circuits (6Pf, 6Ps, 6Pe)
Earth and space: rocks, fossils, soil, the rock cycle, the Solar System and the Moon (6ESp, 6ESc, 6ESs)
Thinking and Working Scientifically: planning investigations, measuring, recording and explaining results (6TWSm, 6TWSp, 6TWSc, 6TWSa)

blocks.text: Written by Mohamed Abdelkriem for students in British and international schools and their parents. Read this page first: it explains the real test, so that every other page in the course makes sense.
What is the Checkpoint 6 Science test?

**Cambridge Primary Checkpoint Science** is a test taken at the **end of Cambridge Primary**, that is, at the end of Stage 6. It is set and marked by Cambridge International, not by your school. The test code is **0097**, the same code as the Stage 6 science curriculum (framework). Older papers with the code 0846 belong to the previous curriculum, so if you practise with them, some topics will be different.

The curriculum has four content strands — **Biology, Chemistry, Physics, Earth and space** — plus **Thinking and Working Scientifically** (how scientists plan, measure and explain). There is also a part called **Science in Context** (how science is used in your area and how scientific ideas change over time). Cambridge says Science in Context is **not directly assessed** in the test, but it helps you understand the topics.

blocks.text: Together the two papers give **80 marks in 70 minutes**. The cover says no additional materials are needed: everything you need (diagrams, tables, graph grids) is printed in the booklet. You write your answers and any working in the spaces in the booklet.

Recent papers have had about **10 to 13 numbered questions**, printed on 16 to 20 pages. Each numbered question is about one context (for example, "Sara investigates how quickly sugar dissolves") and is split into parts **(a), (b), (c), (d)**. A whole question is usually worth 2 to 5 marks. Most parts are worth **1 mark**, and some are worth **2 marks**. The number of marks is printed next to each part, like this: **[1]** or **[2]**.
How to use your 35 minutes

40 marks in 35 minutes means you have about **52 seconds per mark** (35 × 60 = 2100 seconds; 2100 ÷ 40 = 52.5 seconds). That is fast. Checkpoint science questions are short, so you can do it — but only if you do not stop for too long on one part.

items: Read the **context** at the top of each question (the stem). It often contains information you need in part (c) or (d).
Look at the **marks**. [1] = one fact or one word. [2] = two separate points, or a point + a reason.
Answer every part. A blank space can never get a mark; a sensible scientific guess sometimes can.
If a part is hard, write something short, mark it with a small star in the margin, move on, and come back at the end.
Use the last few minutes to check units, ticks (did you tick the right number of boxes?) and graphs (points plotted in pencil, exactly).

blocks.text: Question styles you will meet

Checkpoint Science questions are **context-based**: each question tells a short story about a learner, an investigation or an object. Most questions **mix a content topic with Thinking and Working Scientifically**. For example, a question about dissolving may also ask you to name the independent variable or to spot an anomalous result.

rows: Short answer
"Name the blood vessel that carries blood back to the heart." [1]
One or two words is enough. Spell science words carefully.
Short explanation
"Explain why the ice melts faster on the metal tray." [2]
Give the fact AND the reason (use "because").
Complete the sentence
"Blood carries oxygen from the ______ to the body."
Read the whole sentence after you fill the gap — does it make sense?
Tick or circle one
"Tick (✓) one box." or "Circle the correct word."
Only one or two of these per paper. Tick exactly the number asked for.
Draw lines
Match each word to its meaning with a line.
Use a ruler; one line from each box unless told otherwise.
Tables
Complete a results table, or read a value from it.
Copy numbers carefully; include the unit if the table has no unit in the heading.
Diagrams
Food webs, circuit symbols, force arrows, reading a thermometer.
Draw in pencil, use a ruler for arrows and wires.
Simple calculations
"Work out the change in mass."
Show your working and write the unit.
Investigations
Predict, name the variables, say how to make it fair, suggest an improvement.
Use the words from the question: say exactly what to change or keep the same.

blocks.text: Understanding the mark scheme

After the test, examiners mark your answers with a **mark scheme**. Knowing how it works helps you write answers that earn every mark. The mark scheme has four columns: **Question, Answer, Marks, Further information**. The important ideas are below.

rows: Separates different answers that are all correct for the same mark.
There is often more than one right answer — choose the one you are sure of.
Words or units in brackets are not needed for the mark.
But writing them does no harm, and it makes your answer clearer.
underlined word
That exact word is needed.
Learn key words exactly: "capillaries", not "small tubes", when the word is asked for.
accept
Another answer that also gets the mark.
do not accept
A wrong answer that cancels a right one.
Never write two answers "just in case": a wrong one next to a right one can lose the mark.
ignore
Extra words that are not relevant; they do not lose the mark but earn nothing.
Do not waste time writing extra.
ecf (error carried forward)
If you made a mistake in one part and use your wrong answer correctly in the next part, you can still get the next mark. This is sometimes called "follow through".
Always try the next part, even if you think your first answer was wrong.
ora (or reverse argument)
The opposite way of saying the same thing also gets the mark.
"Metal is a better conductor than wood" = "wood is a worse conductor than metal".
independent marking points
Unless the mark scheme says otherwise, each mark is given separately.
In a [2] answer you can get 1 mark even if the second point is wrong.
show your working
Write the numbers you used, not only the final answer.
If the final answer is wrong, clear working can still help an examiner see what you did.

blocks.text: Two more rules help you: **spelling** — a word spelled the way it sounds still gets the mark, **unless** the spelling turns it into a different science word (for example, "vain" for vein is fine, but writing "artery" when you mean "vein" is simply wrong). **Grammar is not marked** — only the science. Examiners can also use professional judgement for answers that match the marking points in different words.
Worked examples: how marks are given
**Worked example 1** — a 1-mark naming question
Question: Omar boils some water in a kettle. Name the change of state when water turns into water vapour. [1]

rows: evaporation / boiling
Both are accepted: each names a liquid turning into a gas.
evapration
Spelled as it sounds — still clearly the right word.
condensation
Wrong: that is gas turning into liquid.
boiling or condensing
A wrong answer next to a right one contradicts it.

blocks.text: **Common mistake:** writing two answers to be safe. The examiner cannot choose for you.
**Worked example 2** — a 2-mark explanation
Question: Huda puts an ice cube on a metal tray and another ice cube on a plastic tray. The ice on the metal tray melts first. Explain why. [2]

items: Count the marks: [2] means two separate points.
Point 1 (fact): metal is a good **thermal conductor** / plastic is a poor conductor (an insulator).
Point 2 (reason): so heat moves from the warm room, through the metal, into the ice **faster**.
Answer: **"Metal is a better thermal conductor than plastic, so heat travels into the ice faster through the metal tray and it melts sooner."**

blocks.text: **Common mistake:** "Metal is cold." This is not a scientific reason and earns 0. Metal only feels cold because it conducts heat away from your hand quickly.
**Worked example 3** — a calculation with error carried forward

Question: A bottle of fizzy drink has a mass of 525 g. After the lid is opened and the gas escapes for an hour, its mass is 518 g. (a) Work out the change in mass. [1] (b) Explain what your answer tells you about gases. [1]

items: (a) 525 − 518 = **7 g** (write the unit).
(b) The mass went down because gas left the bottle, so **gas has mass**.

If a student wrote 525 − 518 = 17 g in part (a) (a mistake), they lose the mark in (a), but in (b) "the mass decreased because gas (with mass) escaped" still earns the mark — the mistake is not punished twice (ecf).

blocks.text: How results are reported

Your papers are sent to Cambridge and marked there. Each learner then receives a **statement of achievement**, and the school receives a **diagnostic feedback report**. Results are reported for the subject as a whole and for each strand (for example, how well you did in Biology compared with Physics). This shows your teachers and parents which areas are strong and which need more practice.

blocks.title: For parents
blocks.text: The diagnostic feedback report is very useful: it shows strengths and weaknesses by strand. Ask the school to share it, and use the matching section of this course (Biology, Chemistry, Physics, Earth and space) to practise the weaker strand.
Thinking and Working Scientifically (TWS)

TWS is not a separate topic — it is in almost every Checkpoint question. It has four parts. The page **Thinking and Working Scientifically** in this course teaches each one with many examples; here is the big picture.

rows: Models and representations
Use models and diagrams to explain ideas.
Drawing the particles in a solid and a liquid; a model of the Sun, Earth and Moon.
Purpose and planning
Ask questions, predict, plan a fair test, think about risks.
"I predict sugar dissolves faster in hot water because the particles move faster."
Carrying out enquiry
Choose equipment, measure accurately, repeat, record in tables, use keys and secondary sources.
Use a thermometer to measure water temperature to the nearest 1 °C, three times.
Analysis, evaluation and conclusions
Describe patterns, spot anomalous results, conclude, suggest improvements, draw graphs.
"As the temperature increases, the time to dissolve decreases. The result at 40 °C is anomalous."

blocks.text: Scientists use **five main types of scientific enquiry**. You must know what each one is and choose the right one for a question:

rows: Fair testing
Change one variable, measure another, keep everything else the same.
Does the temperature of water change how fast salt dissolves?
Observing over time
Watch and record the same thing changing over minutes, days or months.
How does the Moon's shape change over one month?
Pattern seeking
Collect data from many things you cannot control, then look for a pattern.
Do people who exercise more have a lower resting heart rate?
Identifying and classifying
Sort things into groups using their features; use or make a key.
Which of these rocks are igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic?
Research
Use secondary sources (books, reliable websites, experts) to find answers you cannot test yourself.
How did scientists find out that the heart pumps blood around the body?

blocks.text: How to use this course

The course follows the Stage 6 curriculum strand by strand. Each lesson page has the objectives, key words with Arabic meanings, clear diagrams, worked examples, common mistakes, exam tips and an interactive practice quiz with full solutions. At the end there are three full practice tests in the Checkpoint style (Paper 1 and Paper 2, 35 minutes and 40 marks each).

blocks.text: A suggested study plan (about 12 weeks before the test, two short sessions a week):

items: **Week 1:** this page and Thinking and Working Scientifically. Learn the variables words by heart.
**Weeks 2–4:** Biology pages (one or two a week).
**Weeks 5–6:** Chemistry pages.
**Weeks 7–8:** Physics pages.
**Week 9:** Earth and space pages.
**Weeks 10–12:** one practice test each week, timed (35 minutes per paper). After each test, mark it, write down every topic where you lost marks, and go back to that page.
**Every session:** read the page, cover the key words and test yourself, then do the quiz without looking. Redo any wrong question a few days later.

blocks.title: Common mistakes in Checkpoint Science
items: Writing two answers "to be safe" — a wrong answer next to a right one loses the mark.
Giving only one point for a [2] question — two marks need two separate ideas.
Forgetting units: 7 is not an answer; 7 g is.
Using everyday words instead of science words: "the heart pushes blood" is fine, but "blood goes in the tubes" is too vague when the question wants "arteries" or "veins".
Ignoring the context: if the question is about Sara's experiment with sugar, your answer must be about sugar and water, not a general rule.
Leaving a blank. Always write something scientific.

blocks.title: How Checkpoint asks this
items: The command word tells you what to do: **Name** = a word or short phrase; **Describe** = say what happens or what the pattern is; **Explain** = say why (use "because"); **Predict** = say what you think will happen; **Suggest** = use your knowledge in a new situation — any sensible scientific idea can score.
Most questions mix a topic with investigation skills. Revise the variables words for every topic.
Tables and graphs appear in most questions: practise reading values and describing patterns ("as … increases, … decreases").
Diagrams must be drawn in pencil with a ruler: circuit symbols, force arrows, food web arrows.
Calculations are short (for example, a change in mass or temperature) — show the subtraction and write the unit.

blocks.title: نصيحة مهمة
blocks.text: امتحان Checkpoint Science فيه ورقتين، كل ورقة ٣٥ دقيقة و٤٠ درجة. اقرأ القصة اللي في أول كل سؤال كويس، وبص على عدد الدرجات: لو السؤال عليه درجتين يبقى لازم تكتب فكرتين. ما تكتبش إجابتين مختلفتين عشان "تضمن" — الإجابة الغلط جنب الصح بتضيع الدرجة. واكتب الوحدة دايمًا (g, cm, °C).

blocks.title: Checkpoint 6 Science: test facts quiz
blocks.intro: Eight quick questions about the test and the mark scheme. Answer them all, then check the solutions.

questions.q: How long is each Checkpoint 6 Science paper?
questions.e: Each of the two papers (0097/01 and 0097/02) lasts 35 minutes.

questions.q: Each paper is worth 40 marks. How many marks are there in total for the two papers?
A paper has 40 marks and lasts 35 minutes. About how many seconds do you have for each mark?
questions.e: 35 minutes = 35 × 60 = 2100 seconds. 2100 ÷ 40 = 52.5 seconds per mark (about 52 or 53 seconds).

questions.q: Which part of the Stage 6 curriculum is NOT directly assessed in the Checkpoint test?
questions.e: Cambridge says Science in Context is not directly assessed. Thinking and Working Scientifically is tested in almost every question.

questions.q: In a mark scheme, what do the letters ecf stand for?
questions.e: ecf = error carried forward: if you use a wrong earlier answer correctly in a later part, you can still get the later mark.

questions.q: Leila wants to answer this question: "Do children with longer legs jump further?" She measures the leg length and the jump distance of 30 children. Which type of enquiry is this?
questions.e: She cannot control leg length, so she cannot do a fair test. She collects data from many children and looks for a pattern — pattern seeking.

questions.q: Which pencil does the paper tell you to use for diagrams and graphs?
questions.e: Answers are written in black or dark blue pen; an HB pencil is used for diagrams and graphs.

questions.q:
The question is: "Name the gas that moves from the air into the blood in the lungs." [1]
Yusuf writes: "oxygen / carbon dioxide". Explain why Yusuf gets no mark.
questions.ms: 1 mark: he gave a wrong answer (carbon dioxide) as well as the right one (oxygen); the wrong answer contradicts / cancels the right one. Accept: "he wrote two answers and one is wrong." Do not accept: "his spelling is wrong".
questions.e: Oxygen is correct, but carbon dioxide is wrong (it moves the other way, out of the blood). When you give a right and a wrong answer together, the wrong one contradicts the right one, so no mark is given. Always write one answer.

blocks.title: Remember
items: Two papers, 35 minutes and 40 marks each — a little more than one mark a minute.
Answer on the paper in black or dark blue pen; diagrams and graphs in HB pencil. Paper 1 allows a calculator.
Look at the marks: [2] means two points. Give one answer only — never a right and a wrong one together.
Most questions mix a topic with investigation skills: variables, fair tests, tables, graphs, conclusions.
Results are reported for the whole subject and for each strand, with a feedback report for your school.
